query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn system was selected to reduce cost while retaining the mechanical performance of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi; prior work reported comparable or better mechanical properties after excluding Co. Research on FeNiCrMn has mainly addressed corrosion, while studies of related high- and medium-entropy alloys examined dynamic responses under tension or compression, different temperatures and strain rates, compositional changes, and the presence of cracks or voids. Those studies established that dynamic properties are sensitive to loading regime and material condition, but their different chemistries and defect states do not identify what governs FeNiCrMn. Under the constraints of retaining the Co-free composition and its strength–ductility balance, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains the dynamic behavior of solidified FeNiCrMn across temperature and strain-rate regimes? Define a controlled study capable of testing the hypothesis, its applicable boundaries, the prior findings that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The dynamic mechanical response of solidified, Co‐free FeNiCrMn is governed by a temperature‐dependent transition in dislocation dynamics: at low temperatures and high strain rates, limited thermal activation boosts dislocation drag and accumulation leading to enhanced yield strength and strain hardening, while at higher temperatures dynamic recovery processes become dominant, mitigating dislocation buildup yet preserving ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: Solidified, homogenized equiatomic FeNiCrMn alloy with a controlled, minimal-defect microstructure that retains the inherent strength–ductility balance.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to a matrix of tensile and compressive tests across a broad temperature range (e.g., 77 K to 600 K) and a wide spectrum of strain rates (from quasi-static around 10^(-4) s^(-1) to dynamic >10^3 s^(-1)), complemented by dislocation dynamics simulations.
generation.conditions: Identical alloy composition and microstructure maintained throughout; tests performed under controlled thermal environments and loading conditions with measures of dislocation density and morphology via TEM/XRD.
generation.structural_mediator: The density and evolution of dislocations, including their nucleation, drag, and recovery (recovery processes that re-establish equilibrium dislocation configurations at higher temperatures).
generation.mechanism: At low temperatures and high strain rates, reduced thermal activation limits dislocation mobility, causing dislocation drag and accumulation that increase yield strength and strain-hardening rate. Conversely, at higher temperatures, enhanced dislocation mobility enables dynamic recovery, which lowers dislocation drag and yield strength without sacrificing ductility, thus maintaining the overall balanced properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Experiments and simulations will show that yield strength and strain-rate sensitivity are significantly higher at low temperatures under dynamic conditions due to dislocation drag, while elevated temperatures shift the mechanism toward dynamic recovery, reducing yield strength and altering work-hardening behavior. Post-deformation microstructural analysis should reveal higher dislocation densities and less recovery at low temperatures relative to higher temperatures at comparable strain rates.
generation.baseline: Behavior measured under quasi-static loading at ambient temperature, where the strength–ductility balance is well established for the Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies exclusively to solidified, Co-free FeNiCrMn alloys with controlled microstructures. It excludes influences from additional compositional modifications (e.g., introduction of Co or other alloying elements) or extrinsic defect states such as significant porosity or second-phase precipitates.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty in the precise temperature and strain rate thresholds where the transition from dislocation-drag dominance to dynamic recovery occurs, and in quantifying the contribution of other possible mechanisms (such as deformation-induced twinning) under extreme conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare homogenized samples of the FeNiCrMn alloy and perform a series of tensile and compressive tests at several controlled temperatures (e.g., 77 K, 300 K, 600 K) and strain rates (from 10^(-4) s^(-1) to above 10^3 s^(-1)). In parallel, conduct dislocation dynamics simulations using the initial microstructure as input. Use in situ and post-mortem TEM/XRD analyses to quantify dislocation density and morphology.
measurements: Microstructural evolution indicators (e.g., signs of dynamic recovery vs. dislocation accumulation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimental data do not exhibit the predicted increase in yield strength and strain-rate sensitivity at low temperatures with high dislocation accumulation, or if dynamic recovery does not become the dominant mechanism at elevated temperatures (as evidenced by dislocation density and morphology), then the hypothesis would be falsified. Alternatively, if other deformation mechanisms (such as twinning or phase transformation) are found to control the dynamic response, this would also falsify the hypothesis.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are new alloys that contain five or more elements in roughly-equal proportion. We present new experiments and theory on the deformation behavior of HEAs under slow stretching (straining), and observe differences, compared to conventional alloys with fewer elements. For a specific range of temperatures and strain-rates, HEAs deform in a jerky way, with sudden slips that make it difficult to precisely control the deformation. An analytic model explains these slips as avalanches of slipping weak spots and predicts the observed slip statistics, stress-strain curves, and their dependence on temperature, strain-rate, and material composition. The ratio of the weak spots’ healing rate to the strain-rate is the main tuning parameter, reminiscent of the Portevin-LeChatellier effect and time-temperature superposition in polymers. Our model predictions agree with the experimental results. The proposed widely-applicable deformation mechanism is useful for deformation control and alloy design.

The effect of changing temperatures and adding elements to alloys ranging from FCC-LEAs to FCC-HEAs has been studied to investigate the PLC effect at a strain-rate of 10−4/s. The effect of varying the strain-rates from 1 × 10−5 to 1 × 10−2/s on the serration behavior was examined. The PLC effect is observed in a specific range of temperatures and strain-rates for MEAs and HEAs, and not in LEAs representing the conventional substitutional alloys. As shown in the above six observations, the experimental results agree with the model introduced above. Although the pinning mechanism of such alloys is different from that in conventional alloys with low solute contents, their serrations can be explained as avalanches of slipping weak spots. The main difference is that in MEAs and HEAs, the weak spots (or dislocations) weaken upon slipping and re-strengthen (or in-situ pin) at a relatively fast healing rate between avalanches, compared to conventional alloys. In addition, the PLC effect is more pronounced in HEAs than in MEAs.
